summary: Gives a functional specification of the Maximum Allocation with Reservation (MAR) bandwidth constraints model for Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering. It covers assumptions, applicability and worked examples, and compares MAR's performance against criteria for choosing a model. The document is experimental.

eli5.summary: Sharing a pizza, each friend gets a guaranteed slice, but extra slices can be handed out when someone is not hungry. This memo describes a bandwidth-sharing rule for networks that works like that.

subtitle: A bandwidth allocation model that reserves protection for each class while sharing available space.

tldr.problem: The Maximum Allocation Model provides class isolation or efficiency, but not both. Networks need to reserve bandwidth for premium traffic while allowing full sharing under normal load.
tldr.mechanism: MAR assigns each class a bandwidth guarantee and a shared pool. When a class exceeds its guarantee, it can still use spare bandwidth unless unreserved bandwidth drops below a threshold, protecting other classes.
tldr.outcome: MAR achieves bandwidth efficiency, isolation, and QoS protection simultaneously, with simulation showing better performance than MAM and simpler operation than Russian Doll Model.

today: RFC 4126 is an Experimental specification. MAR is one of three bandwidth constraints models for DS-TE (alongside MAM and RDM). It has been used in some research and experimental deployments to balance bandwidth efficiency and class isolation, though production adoption has been limited as networks often choose between MAM's simplicity and RDM's more sophisticated isolation guarantees.

sections.title: Bandwidth Allocation with Reservation and Sharing
sections.content:
Maximum Allocation with Reservation (MAR) is a Bandwidth Constraints Model for Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering that improves on the basic Maximum Allocation Model (MAM) by adding bandwidth reservation mechanisms.

Like MAM, MAR assigns each Class-Type a bandwidth constraint (guarantee). Unlike MAM, MAR allows classes to exceed their guarantees and use spare bandwidth during normal, non-congested conditions. When the network becomes congested, a reservation bandwidth threshold on each link prevents classes that have exceeded their guarantee from accessing the last reserve of capacity, protecting other classes from starvation.

The model provides three goals simultaneously: bandwidth efficiency (full sharing under normal load), bandwidth isolation (preventing one class from starving others under overload), and QoS protection (maintaining service levels for high-priority classes).
sections.eli5: Each type of traffic gets a guaranteed slice of the bandwidth. If the link is not full, any class can borrow unused slices. But once things get tight, classes can only use what they guaranteed themselves or what they already claimed.

sections.title: MAR Model Definition
sections.content:
MAR defines the following per Class-Type and link:

  • BCck: Bandwidth Constraint for Class-Type c on link k. Each class has a guaranteed allocation.
  • RBW_THRESk: Reservation bandwidth threshold on link k. A small amount of bandwidth (typically 1% of link capacity) that is reserved.
  • RESERVED_BWck: Current reserved bandwidth in Class-Type c.
  • UNRESERVED_BWk: Available bandwidth on the link not yet reserved to any class.

The admission rule for a new LSP requesting bandwidth DBW on Class-Type c is:

  • If RESERVED_BWck ≤ BCck (class is within its guarantee): admit if DBW ≤ UNRESERVED_BWk.
  • If RESERVED_BWck > BCck (class exceeded its guarantee): admit if DBW ≤ UNRESERVED_BWk - RBW_THRESk.

This is equivalent to: admit if DBW ≤ UNRESERVED_BWck, where UNRESERVED_BWck accounts for whether the class is over its guarantee.

Best-effort traffic has BCck = 0 and can use any available bandwidth.
sections.eli5: Two rules: if a class has not used up its guarantee, it can grab any free bandwidth. If it has, it can only grab free bandwidth if plenty remains (above the threshold).

sections.title: Setting Bandwidth Constraints
sections.content:
For normal-priority Class-Types, the bandwidth constraint BCck is set proportionally based on forecast or measured traffic load. The proportion is: BCck = (TRAF_LOAD_BWck / SUM(TRAF_LOAD_BWc)) × MAX_RESERVABLE_BWk.

For high-priority Class-Types (voice, critical data), the constraint is set to a multiple of the proportional bandwidth, for example BCck = FACTOR × PROPORTIONAL_BWck, where FACTOR is typically 2 or 3. This over-allocation gives priority to high-priority classes in the reservation rules. High-priority allocations should be 10–15% of link bandwidth at most.

For best-effort Class-Types, BCck = 0, allowing them to fill any unused capacity but losing bandwidth to higher priorities during congestion.
sections.eli5: Allocate bandwidth proportionally to each type of traffic based on expected load. Give high-priority traffic extra guarantees. Best-effort gets nothing guaranteed.

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.content:
Consider a 100-unit link with three Class-Types:

  • BC0 = 30, BC1 = 20, BC2 = 20
  • RBW_THRES = 10

Under normal load, all three classes coexist. Now suppose the link is under heavy load:

  • RESERVED_BW0 = 50 (CT0 exceeded its guarantee of 30)
  • RESERVED_BW1 = 30 (CT1 exceeded its guarantee of 20)
  • RESERVED_BW2 = 10 (CT2 within its guarantee of 20)
  • UNRESERVED_BW = 10

A 5-unit LSP arrives for CT0. Since RESERVED_BW0 (50) > BC0 (30) and 5 > UNRESERVED_BW (10) - RBW_THRES (10), the request is rejected.

A 5-unit LSP for CT2 arrives. Since RESERVED_BW2 (10) ≤ BC2 (20) and 5 ≤ UNRESERVED_BW (10), it is admitted. CT2 can access the free bandwidth because it is still within its guarantee.
sections.eli5: When congestion hits, classes that have used up their guarantee cannot take the last 10 units. Classes still within their guarantee can. This protects everyone fairly.

sections.title: Performance and Applicability
sections.content:
Modeling and simulation show that MAR meets all bandwidth constraints objectives: it works with or without preemption, provides bandwidth efficiency under normal load and isolation under overload, and protects high-priority classes from QoS degradation. Simulation on a 135-node national network shows that under six-times focused overload, MAR loses less traffic than Maximum Allocation Model, with better isolation for premium voice and data.

MAR assumes that Connection Admission Control allocates bandwidth based on measured or forecasted traffic load, and that capacity is adjusted periodically (hours to months) as load changes. MAR is applicable to networks where traffic prediction and capacity planning are practiced. The model is reasonably simple, requiring no new IGP extensions and minimal signaling overhead.

Appendix B discusses bandwidth prediction techniques for path computation.
sections.eli5: Tests show that MAR shares bandwidth well when the network is quiet, protects traffic when busy, and is simple enough for operators to understand and tune.
